source.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE reconstructions and error terms in feature-steering experiments, but does not test whether the error term is structured, pathological relative to random errors, or necessary to preserve model behavior.
record.gate_note: The study reports layer-wise percent loss recovered by SAE reconstructions, which measures reconstruction performance but does not compare SAE errors with random errors of the same size. It also retains the error term while steering features, without a condition that removes it. Steering outcomes therefore do not test whether that term carries function.
record.test_reason: InterPLM trains SAEs on ESM-2-8M and keeps the error term during steering, following Templeton et al. It never analyses the error vector. It reports no linear predictability, no error scaling across SAE sizes, no comparison with random errors of equal norm, no ablation of the error term, and no architecture comparison of dark matter. Percent loss recovered (Table 1) only measures reconstruction quality.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAEs extract many interpretable biological features from ESM-2, far more than neurons, which suggests superposition. Feature activations can flag missing annotations, and feature steering can causally influence predictions. They note steering was tested on only a few constrained sequences.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains SAEs on protein-model embeddings and uses feature clamping for steering, recombining the modified reconstruction with the error term. It does not apply a dark-matter analysis or compare error structure across SAE sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effects are reported for selected glycine-related features and constrained sequences; the authors note that only a few such sequences were tested.

fits_no_version.finding: Layer-wise percent loss recovered for the selected SAEs on ESM-2-8M is 98.4–100% (Appendix B.1, Table 1). The reference is zero-ablated embeddings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard L1 SAEs on small protein LM embeddings recover nearly all cross-entropy relative to zero ablation.

record.problems: For the dark-matter claim, the study does not compare SAE error to random errors, measure error predictability or scaling, or ablate the error term in steering. The loss-recovery metric is reported without uncertainty.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from input activations.
Per-token error-norm prediction across SAE sizes; overlap of failure contexts across sizes; persistence of error with scale. Only one dictionary size (10,240) was used per layer.
Loss increase from SAE reconstruction compared with random errors of equal norm.
Content and learnability of the linear versus nonlinear error components.
Steering keeps the error term throughout. No condition omits it, so the loss of behaviour without it is not measured.
Effect of SAE training choices or architectures on dark matter. The 20-run hyperparameter sweep was selected on Swiss-Prot F1 and is not reported as error analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The study's subject is a protein masked language model rather than a text LM. The error term appears only as a retained component in steering (Methods 5.5); nothing about it is measured.

versions.untested_parts: Whether SAE error vectors are linearly predictable from input activations.
Error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap of failure contexts across sizes, and whether error persists with scale.
Whether reconstruction replacement harms model loss more than random errors of equal size.
Whether the linear and nonlinear error components differ in feature content or learnability.
Whether steering or other analyses lose behavior when the error term is omitted.
Whether training choices or improved SAE architectures account for dark matter or make it shrink.
